topics.topic: Authoritative declaration and pinning of operation effect classes
questions: Where is an operation's effect class declared, who is allowed to choose it, and what prevents an agent from proposing a dangerous operation as read-only?
Where is an operation's effect class declared, who is authorized to assign it, what does a binding pin about it, and what happens if it is missing or changes?
Where is an operation node's effect class declared, who is authorized to set it, and what immutable record does a flow proof rely on?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about the manifest being authoritative for effect classes and preventing proposer-supplied classifications.

precedent.topic: Authority, storage, and integrity of operation effect-class assignments
quotes:
The proposer
   names only service, operation and ports; effect class and key fields are
   copied from the manifest (M11).

A proposal that states its own effect class is refused; the manifest's class is
   the binding's.
precedent.why: State 2 makes the manifest authoritative and prevents the agent from supplying the effect class or key declaration.

topics.topic: Effect of corpus growth on an already admitted active implementation
questions: When a case is added after an implementation was admitted and activated, is that implementation automatically re-admitted, deactivated until re-submitted, or allowed to remain active under an obsolete verdict?

When a trial case is added or captured after the current implementation was admitted, is that implementation re-admitted, deactivated, allowed to keep running under its old verdict, or is corpus mutation refused until another implementation is admitted?
When the corpus changes, are old admission verdicts invalidated, is the active implementation automatically re-tested, and what happens if it fails the enlarged corpus?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about corpus growth, verdict coverage and the continued service of an active implementation.

precedent.topic: Effect of trial-corpus changes on admitted and active implementations
quotes:
The corpus of a contract version is its
   cases in the order they were first added — the store's order (K-17).

Capturing a failed execution (M06 rule, State 0 action) adds a case and so
   changes the corpus digest; the serving implementation keeps serving. It
   visibly lacks a verdict over the current corpus when the slot is inspected,
   and serves until another implementation is activated.
precedent.why: State 2 makes every added case part of the corpus, invalidates current-corpus verdict coverage, and deliberately leaves the current implementation serving.

topics.topic: Guard data model, comparisons, branches, and unmatched outcomes
questions: What does a guard compare, how are its branches declared, and what observable result occurs when no branch matches?
What is a declared closed value, what comparison is performed, which nodes or edges the guard controls, and what trace/output is produced for the branch not taken?
What is the exact data model and runtime behavior of a guard?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about guard representation, selection, skipped branches, traces and outputs.

precedent.topic: Guard inputs, branch representation, unmatched values, skipped nodes, and outputs
quotes:
The
  node runs once per element in list order (a `many` value is a list); every other input is given the
  same value for every element; each output collects one result per element in
  that order.

A node whose every incoming edge is disabled by its guard is not
  executed and is recorded `skipped_by_guard`;

A mapped node,
   once selected, takes its elements in list order, each once in the pass, and
   runs every one that has no concluded record and does not wait — a concluded element is never executed again — before the next node is
   selected; an element that waits or fails does not stop the elements after it.
precedent.why: The later models and run rules define map ordering, per-element behavior, guard matching, skipped branches, and failure propagation.

topics.topic: Idempotency-key declaration, placement, derivation, and reuse semantics
questions: What declares whether and where an operation accepts the idempotency key, and what happens when an effectful operation has no valid declaration?
Where and how does an operation declare support for the idempotency key, how is the key inserted into the request, and what happens when an effectful operation has no valid declaration?
What uniquely determines an idempotency key, where is it placed in the request, how long is it retained, and is the same key reused after `not_applied` resolution?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about idempotency-key declaration, transport, derivation, persistence and resend identity.

precedent.topic: Idempotency-key declaration, generation, transport, persistence, and retry identity
quotes:
The key travels to the service as those input fields themselves, in
   the places A09 rule 2 gives them; the kernel adds no header or field of its own
   (K-08: "the declared idempotency key"). The EffectAttempt's `idempotency_key`
   is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of those fields' values, and absent when
   the manifest declares none.

A `not_sent` attempt leaves its approval
unused (M24), so a resume sends a new attempt under it. Sending again after `not_applied` is a new attempt
under a fresh approval, never under a standing approval (K-08).
precedent.why: Later states define declaration, placement, derivation, persistence, attempt scope, and resend behavior.

topics.topic: Mapping primary actions onto the fixed MCP operation surface
questions: How are the separately promised actions add a trial case, capture a failed execution, release a failed run, roll back a slot and propose a binding exposed on MCP?

Which MCP operations carry add-trial-case, capture-failed-execution, release-failed-run, rollback-slot, propose-binding, and compose-and-prove-flow, all of which are primary actions but are absent from the declared fixed surface?
Are those primary actions separate MCP operations, or which named K-11 operation carries each one and preserves its distinct authorization and result?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about mapping every primary action to the fixed MCP operation catalogue.

precedent.topic: MCP operations corresponding to primary actions omitted from the fixed surface
quotes:
The one fixed set of typed operations over `mcp` (K-11), one per State 0
action.

| `add_trial_case` | author | `functions.add_trial_case` |
| `submit_implementation` | author | `functions.submit_implementation` |
| `try_implementation` | agent | `functions.try_implementation` |
| `capture_failed_execution` | owner, author | `runs.capture_failed_execution` |
| `roll_back_slot` | owner, author | `functions.roll_back_slot` |
| `propose_binding` | agent | `bindings.propose_binding` |
| `accept_binding` | owner | `bindings.accept_binding` |
| `compose_flow_version` | agent | `flows.compose_flow_version` |
| `prove_flow_version` | agent | `flows.prove_flow_version` |
| `activate_flow_version` | owner, agent (`read` only, A06) | `flows.activate_flow_version` |

| `release_run` | owner, agent | `runs.release_run` |
| `decide_effect_approval` | owner | `runs.continue_after_approval` |
precedent.why: The State 5 catalogue names the individual MCP operation for every questioned action and permits agent activation of read-only versions.

topics.topic: Owner authentication channel and token lifecycle
questions: Is the owner a distinct MCP caller whose client keeps the owner token from the language-model agent, or does an agent relay owner requests and responses while possessing that token?
Where is the owner token configured, how is it rotated or revoked, and when does a change take effect?

What is the “agent channel,” can its agent or operator observe or reuse the owner token and owner-only responses, and how does the kernel distinguish an owner request from an agent presenting that token?
Who creates, stores, rotates and revokes the owner token, and what observable refusal occurs when it is absent, invalid or revoked?
How is the owner token provisioned, validated, rotated and revoked, and how is it distinguished from an agent token?

quotes:
The installation's configuration file holds the owner token; the agent tokens;
   the selected manifest instance name of each service it selects one for; at
   most one credential for each service it gives one: a header name — an HTTP
   field-name token, or the kernel refuses to start — and the reference that
   resolves to its value on the host: the absolute path of a secret file, or
   the kernel refuses to start (a service with none fails only its own
   requests, rule 2); and the
   address the kernel's one `mcp` entrance listens on, which the host's reverse
   proxy reaches (owner, 2026-10-03, raised by the pre-contract data closure).

Before evaluating each request the kernel reads the configuration file and
   compares the SHA-256 of its bytes with that of the last read; when they differ,
   or the file cannot be read, it re-reads it (K-15) and takes from it only the
   token list.

authenticate_token: [SECURITY_BOUNDARY] MUST obtain the token list from current_token_list on every call, and answer None when it returns None, when presented_token is None, or when presented_token equals no token of that list; the comparison is constant-time with the hmac compare_digest function against the owner token and against every agent token, all of them compared whatever an earlier comparison found (A16 rules 1 and 2).

authenticate_token: [RETURN_SHAPE] Returns an Actor of kind owner with no agent_name for the owner token, an Actor of kind agent with the agent_name of the matching AgentToken for an agent token, or None; never an Actor of kind kernel.
| `unauthorized` | the one token refusal: missing, unknown or revoked token, or no valid token list (A16 rules 1–2) | the caller fixes its token |
judgement.why: The later installation and API texts make the owner token a configuration-held bearer credential, apply changes on configuration reread, authenticate its presenter as the owner and define the refusal for an invalid token.

topics.topic: Personal-data restrictions on direct service access by agents
questions: May an agent directly receive or read service data classified as personal_data, or is the owner-only rule meant to apply outside the kernel too?
May an agent receive raw personal data directly from a microservice, or is the no-personal-data rule intended to constrain every agent access path, including the newly excluded direct path?
Is the claim that an agent receives personal data only as digest and class limited to values returned through the kernel, or must direct service access enforce it too?

quotes:
An agent never receives a `personal_data` value: wherever the surface would
return one to an agent, it returns the value's digest and class instead. The
owner receives every value. This is one rule of the surface, not a per-agent
ceiling and not a redaction inside each operation.

No authority over how an agent reaches a microservice directly. An agent's own
  access to a service — as for processing a photo (decision 17) — is granted by
  that service and the owner outside the kernel; the kernel neither gives nor
  checks it, and its personal-data promise (K-14) covers what the kernel itself
  returns.
judgement.why: The owner-only disclosure rule governs the kernel surface, while direct service access is explicitly outside that promise and governed by the service and owner.

topics.topic: Trial-case pass criteria, including cases captured from failures
questions: What expected result makes the captured failure into a passable test case: a supplied expected output, a required success with any contract-valid output, or reproduction of a specific verdict?
What expected result is stored when a failed execution is captured, given that the execution produced no successful output, and what exactly makes a later implementation pass that case?

Does a trial case assert an exact expected output, only successful contract-conforming execution, an expected failure class, or another predicate, and how is that predicate obtained when a failed execution is captured?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about the oracle and pass condition of a trial case captured from a failed execution.

precedent.topic: How a captured failed execution obtains an expected passing result
quotes:
A case passes when the execution succeeded and, if the case states expected
   outputs, every output's digest equals the expected one

only an execution of a function node pinned to the
  same contract version that was executed and did not succeed can be captured
precedent.why: State 1 and State 2 define case contents, optional exact-output oracle, captured-case oracle, and capture eligibility.

topics.topic: Versioned and pinned Python runtime and standard-library capabilities
questions: Which Python implementation and version define the language and standard library for admission and later real execution, and may that runtime change while admitted implementations exist?

Which Python implementation and version are admitted and run, which standard-library modules or capabilities remain available despite the no-network/no-clock/no-randomness rules, and is that environment identity pinned with an implementation or run?
Which Python runtime version and standard-library module allowlist define the execution environment, and how are changes to that environment versioned?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about the pinned Python implementation, version, callable interface and permitted standard-library capabilities.

precedent.topic: Pinned Python runtime, callable interface, encoding, and permitted standard-library boundary
quotes:
The runtime is one Python interpreter with its standard library and nothing
   else, fixed by the kernel release (State 0 questions 4 and 17: photo processing
   is the agent's own work outside the kernel), started with a fixed
   hash seed (`PYTHONHASHSEED=0`) so that set and dict ordering repeats. Adding a
   library is a new kernel release.

An implementation is a Python module that defines a top-level function `run`
   taking one argument, a dict with one entry per input port, and returning a dict
   with exactly one entry per output port.

A release pins the exact versions of the kernel's Python dependencies and of
   the sandbox runtime (A03); the sandbox interpreter of release v1 is CPython
   3.12, whose `random` module gives A03 rule 4 its list. A vulnerable dependency is answered by a new
   release; a running kernel never updates one.

Before loading the module, the in-sandbox runner replaces every clock and
   randomness entry point of the standard library (`time`, `datetime` current-time
   functions, `os.urandom`, `random` seeding, `secrets`) with one that raises, and
   installs an audit hook that raises on socket, subprocess, `ctypes` and on
   opening any path outside the exchange directory and the read-only runtime.
precedent.why: Later function, installation and sandbox texts pin the interpreter, callable ABI and standard-library capability restrictions.

topics.topic: Atomic timing of dependency and runtime pinning for a run
questions: Are all function activations, flow bindings, manifest operation digests and service-instance request material pinned atomically when the run starts, or are they pinned when each node becomes ready?
Are all function activations, bindings, manifest records and runtime versions pinned atomically when the run is created, or is each dependency pinned only when its node first executes or resumes?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about the timing and dependency scope of run pinning.

precedent.topic: Atomic timing and full dependency scope of run pinning
quotes:
The run pins the flow version and, for every function node, the implementation
   of the current activation at start (M19). Nothing recorded later — a new
   activation, a new flow activation, a new binding — changes what the run
   executes.

- `binding_id`: present exactly for an operation node — the proof refuses a
  binding that is not `accepted` (K-03);
Before every send, the kernel reads the operation again.

The instance of every service is the one the installation selects (K-16); no
   request, flow or binding chooses another.

A release pins the exact versions of the kernel's Python dependencies and of
   the sandbox runtime (A03); the sandbox interpreter of release v1 is CPython
   3.12, whose `random` module gives A03 rule 4 its list. A vulnerable dependency is answered by a new
   release; a running kernel never updates one.
precedent.why: The later models and rules specify which dependencies are pinned at run start, which are embedded in the immutable flow, which are rechecked before sending, and which are fixed for the process or release.

topics.topic: Authentication and transport security for outbound service connections
questions: How does the kernel authenticate a selected service instance and protect and verify the outbound connection?
What authenticates a microservice endpoint and protects service credentials and data in transit between the kernel and the service?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about outbound endpoint identity, credentials, TLS verification and redirect handling.

precedent.topic: Microservice endpoint identity, transport security and redirect handling
quotes:
An invocation is one HTTP request to the selected instance's `api_base_url`
   joined with the declared path, with the method declared, the instance's
   `required_headers` with their manifest values verbatim — header names compare
   without regard to case, and a record naming one header twice so is a manifest
   mismatch — and the credential
   header the installation holds for that service (A17);

Nothing else is normalized. Redirects are not followed; proxy environment
   variables are ignored; nothing is retried inside one attempt.

TLS is verified for `https`. Plain `http` is allowed only for an instance of
   class `local_dev` or `disposable_rig`, as the manifest instance's `class`
   states — an absent or unknown class counts as `production` — or one whose
   `api_base_url` host is a loopback address; any other plain `http` target is refused before sending.
   The host judged here, the one connected to, and for `https` the server name
   sent and verified, are always those of `api_base_url`; a required `Host`
   header (A10 rule 7) changes only the header sent.
precedent.why: State 2 fixes endpoint selection, credential placement, redirect behavior, TLS verification, plain-HTTP eligibility and server-name identity.

topics.topic: Cancellation behavior and recording for work already in flight
questions: What happens to a function or HTTP request already executing when cancellation is accepted, and how are a late service response or side effect recorded?
Can cancellation interrupt an in-flight call, and how are an already-sent effect and an ambiguous cancellation race recorded?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about cancellation relative to an executing function or outbound request.

precedent.topic: Cancellation semantics for functions and outbound operations already in flight
quotes: Requests are handled strictly one at a time, each to its end, run advancement included, before the next one is read (A18 rule 3).

Cancel, by the owner only, ends a run that has not ended as `cancelled`:
   nothing further is sent, every concluded record stays, undecided approvals can
   no longer be decided, and the spool is emptied.
precedent.why: The single-request execution model prevents cancellation from arriving concurrently with a running function or HTTP send; cancellation applies only after the active request ends.

topics.topic: Definition of schema identity and supported schema representation
questions: What makes two schemas the same: byte identity, canonical structural equality, a schema identifier and version, or equivalence after reference resolution?
What schema representation is supported, and does “same” mean byte identity, canonical structural equality or mutual assignability?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about the supported schema language, canonicalization and equality rule.

precedent.topic: Schema language, canonicalization, and meaning of schema sameness
quotes:
**Supported JSON Schema subset** (A02 rule 1, carried by States 1 and 2): a
   schema is a JSON object using only `type` (one of `null`, `boolean`,
   `integer`, `number`, `string`, `array`, `object`, as one string), `enum`
   (a non-empty array of distinct scalars), `const` (one scalar), `properties`
   and `required` (for `object`), `additionalProperties` (`true` or `false`
   only), `items` (one schema, for `array`), `minItems`, `maxItems`,
   `minLength`, `maxLength`, `minimum` and `maximum`.

"The same schema" means
   equal canonical JSON (State 1); two schemas that accept the same values but
   are written differently are different.
precedent.why: State 6 defines the schema language, while State 2 defines canonical equality.

topics.topic: Deterministic selection, ordering, and pagination of repair context
questions: What deterministic bound and ordering define which traces and evidence an agent receives for repair?
What makes traces or trial evidence “recent,” in what deterministic order and quantity are they returned, and can the agent page to older evidence?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about repair-view selection, recency ordering, bounds and pagination.

precedent.topic: Repair-context action, slot selection and bounded recent evidence
quotes: | `get_repair_view` | owner, agent | one slot's repair read (A15 rule 6, K-12), not a list operation of A16 rule 6: `functions.read_slot`; the current contract version through `functions.read_contract_version` and its whole corpus; the current implementation through `functions.read_implementation`, with code, and its trial executions on the corpus — none, without an error, when the current contract version has no current activation; and through `store.page_records` the latest NodeExecutions of the slot's implementations — `page_size_default` unless the caller asks another size, at most `page_size_max` (A16 rule 6) — with a continuation token that also carries the implementation set of its first page; passed back, it pages only the NodeExecutions below that position for that set — an implementation added since has only newer executions, so nothing below is missed — and every other part is read again as of that request; the token is bound to its slot, so passed with another slot it is `invalid_request`, as the rule below the table says for every continuation token, and only the page size may change |
precedent.why: The State 5 catalogue defines the repair action, authorization, whole corpus, execution evidence, recency order, limits, and pagination.

topics.topic: Disclosure-class assignment for caller-supplied, literal, and zero-input values
questions: Who assigns and validates the class of a flow input, and what class is assigned to output from a function that receives no inputs?
Who assigns and validates the class of a flow input, guard value, literal or other value not returned by a service or derived from function inputs?
What disclosure class does a function output receive when the function has no inputs, or receives no value because an optional or empty mapped input is absent?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about assigning disclosure classes to flow inputs, constants and zero-input function outputs.

precedent.topic: Assignment and propagation of disclosure classes for non-service, absent, and zero-input values
quotes:
At run time a value's class is set by the one rule of M21: a flow input takes
   its port's class, a constant its declared class, a function output the highest
   class its execution actually received, a binding output the class the binding
   declares, a trial case's input its contract input port's class and its
   expected output the highest class of the case's inputs.
a function with no inputs yields `open`.

- `value`: a StoredValue (M21) of `value` carriage — a constant is never a file —
  whose class the composing agent declares with the constant.
precedent.why: The later models and disclosure rules assign classes to every value source named by the topic.

topics.topic: Execution and sandbox boundary for agent-written code outside the kernel
questions: Does outside-kernel photo processing permit agent-written code to execute outside the kernel sandbox, and if so, what system executes it and owns that trust boundary?
Does “agent-written code” mean only code submitted as a kernel function, or is outside-the-kernel photo processing also required to run in a sandbox?

quotes: **Agent-written code** — untrusted forever; runs only inside the sandbox.

Photo processing is not a kernel function: the agent processes a photo itself,
    outside the kernel, with its own access to the service that holds the photo —
    never through the kernel, which hands no caller a file — and the kernel moves
    the file between services.
judgement.why: Agent-written code remains sandbox-only, while the separately described photo processing is an action of the agent outside the kernel and is expressly not a kernel function.

topics.topic: Initiation, evidence, and production requirements for effectful-flow rehearsal
questions: Who initiates a rehearsal, what action distinguishes it from an ordinary run, what observable evidence proves it occurred on disposable rigs, and what failure prevents production use if it did not occur?
Who starts a rehearsal, how it differs from an ordinary run, what evidence it produces, and whether successful rehearsal is required before production activation are all unspecified.

quotes:
Effectful flows are rehearsed on an installation of disposable
rigs.

| activate a flow | agent or owner asks; the kernel activates a proven read-only version at once; any other version only when the owner asks | active flow version | an unproven version is refused; an agent asking to activate a version with effects is refused and nothing is kept for the owner — the owner activates it by the same action |
judgement.divergence: One implementer treats rehearsal as an ordinary optional run on a disposable-rig installation and permits owner activation without rehearsal evidence; another records a distinct successful rehearsal and refuses production activation until it exists, which the owner notices as different activation behavior and evidence.
judgement.why: The text requires rehearsal but neither assigns its initiating action and observable evidence nor decides whether it is a prerequisite for activation elsewhere.

topics.topic: Map input, concurrency, ordering, aggregation, and failure semantics
questions: What are the map construct's input and output shapes, ordering rule, concurrency rule, and result when one mapped item fails, waits, is refused or is cancelled?

judgement.why: This is the same unchanged question about mapped-node input shape, order, waiting, approvals, aggregation and failure behavior.

precedent.topic: Map input/output shape, ordering, concurrency, bounds, approvals, and failure semantics
quotes:
The
  node runs once per element in list order (a `many` value is a list); every other input is given the
  same value for every element; each output collects one result per element in
  that order.

A node whose every incoming edge is disabled by its guard is not
  executed and is recorded `skipped_by_guard`;

A mapped node,
   once selected, takes its elements in list order, each once in the pass, and
   runs every one that has no concluded record and does not wait — a concluded element is never executed again — before the next node is
   selected; an element that waits or fails does not stop the elements after it.
precedent.why: The later models and run rules define map ordering, per-element behavior, guard matching, skipped branches, and failure propagation.

precedent.topic: Detection and observable handling of credentials echoed in service responses
quotes:
A 2xx body that echoes it is
   therefore not used: the answer is `contract_violation` (rule 5), no output
   is stored or spooled, and for a non-read operation the attempt is `applied`

Every body as read, whatever its status — reading stops at the ceiling
   (rule 5) — is searched, before it is parsed or cut, for the bytes of the credential
   value sent with the request; when they occur, the body is
   dropped whole and `failure_detail` is exactly `error body withheld: it
   contained the credential`
precedent.why: State 2 defines the node outcome, effect-attempt result, stored failure detail, and absence of output.

quotes:
when nothing can
